 The best fitness trackers do far more than count steps. Today's wearables can help you understand how well you've slept, whether you're recovered enough to train, how your heart is performing and even when it's time to take a rest day. Better still, you don't need to spend flagship smartwatch money to benefit from those insights.
 The category has evolved dramatically over the last few years, too. Alongside familiar fitness bands, you'll now find lightweight GPS watches, discreet smart rings and even screen-free trackers that quietly collect health data without constantly demanding your attention. Choosing the right one is less about finding the device with the longest feature list and more about finding the one that fits your lifestyle.
 Our team has spent more than a decade testing fitness trackers, smartwatches and wearable technology from Garmin , Apple , Fitbit , Samsung , Amazfit and many more. We judge every device on tracking accuracy, battery life, comfort, software, training tools and overall value, wearing each one for weeks before deciding whether it deserves a place in this guide.

 If the idea of wearing a fitness tracker without another screen in your life appeals, the Garmin Cirqa is the best screenless option we've tested. It quietly tracks your activity, sleep and recovery throughout the day, then surfaces everything in the excellent Garmin Connect app when you're ready to check in.
 The Cirqa takes a more hands-off approach to fitness tracking than a smartwatch. It fades into the background between workouts, quietly logging your sleep, heart rate and recovery without another screen demanding your attention. When you do want to exercise, the tactile button makes starting and stopping a workout quick and reassuringly simple, and we found its heart rate and sleep tracking more than capable for day-to-day training.
 It isn't cheap, and for similar money you could pick up an entry-level Garmin watch such as the Forerunner 165 , which offers built-in GPS and more advanced training features. However, if your goal is to spend less time looking at a screen while still benefiting from Garmin's health insights, the Cirqa makes a strong case for itself. 
The free Garmin Connect app includes all the core health and fitness metrics most people need, while the optional Connect+ subscription (£6.99 / $6.99 per month) adds AI-powered insights, extra coaching and a handful of premium features. That also gives the Cirqa an edge over Whoop, whose subscription is mandatory rather than optional, making Garmin's tracker the more affordable choice over the long term.

 How to choose the best fitness tracker 
 When choosing a fitness tracker, start by thinking about how you exercise. If you're mainly interested in tracking daily activity, sleep and general wellness (such as recovery, stress, heart health and overall activity levels), a simple fitness band or screenless tracker may be all you need. However, if you run, cycle or spend a lot of time training outdoors, it's worth looking for a device with built-in GPS so it can accurately track your routes and pace without relying on your phone.
 Next, consider how much data you actually want. Some trackers focus on simple metrics like steps, heart rate and sleep, while others provide detailed training analysis, recovery insights and personalised coaching. More information isn't always better, so think about whether you'll use those extra metrics before paying for them.
 Comfort matters too. A fitness tracker proves the most useful when you wear it consistently, so it's worth considering how it will fit into your everyday life. If you already wear a traditional watch, a smart ring such as the Samsung Galaxy Ring or a screenless tracker like the Google Fitbit Air or Amazfit Helio Strap can be a good alternative, offering health and activity tracking without adding another watch-sized device to your wrist.
 Finally, think about the display. Devices with bright AMOLED screens are generally easier to read at a glance and outdoors in bright sunlight, while simpler fitness bands often prioritise battery life over display quality. If you plan to check your stats regularly throughout the day, a larger, sharper screen may be worth the extra cost.
 What is a fitness tracker?
 A fitness tracker is a device, typically a wristband, that monitors statistics such as your heart rate, the number of steps you take each day, and how long you spend working out. You might think of Fitbit bands as the quintessential tracker, but Apple Watches and other devices, such as smart rings, are fitness trackers too. 
 Most fitness trackers have several dedicated modes for recording different forms of exercise, and some also have GPS for tracking your location during runs, walks and bike rides. Most fitness trackers also monitor how long you spend sleeping, and in each sleep stage.
 All this data is sent to an app on your smartphone, where you can track changes over time. Most apps give you virtual 'awards' for achieving particular goals, such as taking 10,000 steps per day or going to bed on time.
 Why do you need a fitness tracker?
 It can be tough to break old habits and develop new ones, and a fitness tracker can help give you the encouragement you need. Tracking the number of steps you take each day and aiming for a particular target might be simple, but it can push you to make simple changes (like getting off the bus a stop earlier, or walking short distances rather than driving), which can add up to make a significant difference over time.
 Which fitness trackers are most accurate?
 Most modern fitness trackers do an excellent job in tracking heart rate, stress and sleep accurately. Fitness trackers have optical heart rate sensors that can keep up with quick changes in heart rate. 
 Some have GPS to better track running, walking and cycling workouts outdoors. This is generally an estimation, but if you run, walk or cycle frequently and want to closely track those workouts, it's best to choose a tracker with GPS as it can monitor your routes, distance travelled, and speed. 
 Check our full reviews for more information: we test fitness trackers against each other and industry gold standards, such as the Apple Watch Ultra 3 or Polar H10 heart rate monitor , to determine whether there are significant differences in GPS and heart rate readings.
 What makes a good fitness tracker?
 A good fitness tracker is one that you'll wear every day and will help you build up a complete picture of your health. With that knowledge, you can start to make small tweaks that will help you sleep better, lower your resting heart rate, improve your fitness, and generally feel better. 
 How we test the best fitness trackers 
 Battery
 During testing we extensively study the battery life of all these devices. Simply wearing them for a few days isn't enough, so we always make sure to run them down completely to get a true feel for how long battery lasts in a given fitness tracker. Obviously your mileage may vary, but we always use them the way most regular people would to give a fair assessment.
 Health tracking and accuracy
 All of our reviewers have extensive experience with fitness and health tracking tech, so we know what to look for when it comes to calorie tracking, heart rates, and sleep. We even test these devices alongside existing tech to look for disparity and erratic results.
 Workouts
 Obviously, we undertake extensive fitness tracking to test the best fitness trackers, conducting a variety of workouts including running and cycling. All of our reviewers engage in a variety of different sports, together they bring years of experience and a huge variety of disciplines to the table.

 I walked exactly 6,094 steps wearing the Fitbit Edge on my left wrist and the Apple Watch Series 12 on my right wrist to find out which is the more accurate fitness tracker.
 My 55-minute walk also included just under 500 feet of elevation gain with roughly three miles of ground covered. As a control, I separately logged my walk using the Strava app on my iPhone 16 Plus.
 Find the results of my Fitbit Edge versus Apple Watch Series 12 head-to-head fitness tracking performance test below, along with the five biggest takeaways from the data.
 Fitbit Edge vs. Apple Watch 12 
 (Image credit: Dan Bracaglia/Tom's Guide) But first, it's worth calling out key differences in terms of cost, features, and intended user between these two modern devices. For instance, when it comes to full-featured wearables, the Apple Watch 12 is one of the best smartwatches you can buy.
 The Fitbit Edge, meanwhile, has essentially zero smart features, but is still among the best fitness trackers on the market because it offers reliable, distraction-free holistic insights. Cost-wise, the Fitbit Edge starts at $179 , and the Apple Watch 12 starts at $399 .

 While the Apple Watch 12 is for iOS users only, the Fitbit Edge brings Google's best health and fitness features to both Android and iOS devices.
 Ultimately, when it comes to onboard holistic and tracking tech, the two are fairly evenly matched: Both models have GPS, barometric altimeters, and continuous heart rate monitors.

 1. Fitbit's step count is closer to the control 
 (Image credit: Dan Bracaglia/Tom's Guide) I walked precisely 6,094 steps during my 55-minute outing, according to the control data logged by Strava, a tally that the Fitbit Edge came ridiculously close to matching.
 In terms of accuracy in these comparisons, my rule of thumb is that any step count within 100 steps of the control is excellent and well within a reasonable margin of error. With that in mind, Apple and Fitbit each performed seriously well. But while Apple undercounted by only 41 steps, the Fitbit Edge came within 15 steps of my actual total.
 What to read next

 I walked 10,000 steps with the Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Garmin Fenix 9 Pro — and I was not expecting this 
 2. But Apple's total distance is more accurate 
 (Image credit: Dan Bracaglia/Tom's Guide) On the flip side, when it came to correctly logging my total distance, the Apple Watch Series 12 proved more accurate than the Fitbit Edge, with a tally that's just 0.06 miles off from Strava's measure.
 The Fitbit Edge didn't do too badly, though, coming within 0.13 miles of the control data, a result I still deem more than acceptable.
 3. Fitbit's climb data is spot-on 
 (Image credit: Dan Bracaglia/Tom's Guide) I just published my Fitbit Edge review , and one of the upgrades I'm most excited for is the onboard barometric altimeter for precise elevation tracking. The Edge's predecessor, 2023's Fitbit Charge 6 , lacked this important piece of tech. While some wearables try to roughly calculate climb using GPS data, the Charge 6 never did.
 The upgrade definitely paid off, because the Fitbit Edge logs uphill efforts with impressive reliability. For this test, the Edge's climb data is within four feet of the control. The Apple Watch 12, meanwhile, proved a little more generous with its climb data, a trend I've noted several times before in similar head-to-heads.
 4. Apple's average heart rate is slightly higher than expected 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) I'm not sure if the Apple Watch 12 wasn't worn tightly enough (or maybe too tightly), but the logged average heart rate of 133 bpm for this brisk yet not overly demanding walk is slightly higher than I expected, especially when compared to heart rate data from walks of similar effort (~120 bpm tends to be my average).
 That said, the Fitbit Edge's average heart rate is slightly lower than anticipated, though the max pace is much more aligned with what I've come to expect from such a workout.
 5. Apple's pace is closer to the control, but Fitbit wins overall 
 (Image credit: Dan Bracaglia/Tom's Guide) Finally, Apple's average pace data is much more closely aligned with Strava's. Fitbit's tally, meanwhile, I'd label as "slower than expected," especially given the fact that I was moving briskly and barely paused at any point during the walk.
 That said, the Edge logged several additional minutes of workout time compared to Strava and Apple (it was the last device I ended my workout on), which might be the reason for the sluggishness.
 Ultimately, pace aside, I'm calling the Fitbit Edge the winner for this head-to-head fitness tracking showdown versus the Apple Watch Series 12. Not only did the Edge log a more accurate step count, but it also beat Apple at logging my climb and heart rate (even if the Apple Watch was closer in terms of distance and pace).
 Of course, I'd happily trust either device as my daily fitness tracker. Which begs the question: Which of these two 2026 wearables would you rather own? Let me know in the poll below.

In the past year alone, Dan has assessed major product releases from the likes of Apple, Garmin, Google, Samsung, Polar and many others. 
 An avid outdoor adventurer, Dan is based in the U.S. Pacific Northwest where he takes advantage of the beautiful surroundings every chance he gets. A lover of kayaking, hiking, swimming, biking, snowboarding and exploring, he also makes every effort to combine his day job with his passions.  Though 2026 has been a tumultuous time for technology when it comes to price hikes and shortages, the tech that's reached us has been excellent — in fact, it's been a banner year in most areas, just with some downsides for your wallet.
 We've already crowned the best tech of the year as chosen by you in our TechRadar Readers' Choice Awards 2026 — but this is where we let our experts have their say.
 Our writers and editors chose their favorite products in nearly 100 categories, ranging across all the kinds of products we review. In some cases, we agree with the readers; in lots of cases, we don't. So read on to see which gadgets we rate as being the most impressive of the last 12 months.
 Latest Videos From TechRadar 
 Watch full video here: 
 Phones & tablets 
 Phone of the Year
 Apple iPhone 18 Pro 
 Wherever you look, the iPhone 18 Pro excels. It might not have the biggest camera sensor or the longest-lasting battery of any phone on the market, but it does offer a near-unrivaled combination of premium flagship features. From its variable aperture feature and pro-level video capabilities to its phenomenal performance and gorgeous display, the 18 Pro is the Swiss Army knife of 2026 smartphones.
 Read our full iPhone 18 Pro review 
 Phone Brand of the Year
 Honor 
 The Chinese company has brought something competitive to the table at every turn in 2026. The Honor Magic 8 Pro is an extremely capable flagship. The Magic V6 is easily one of the best foldables you can buy. The Honor 600 series offers some serious value for money in the mid-range sector. The MagicPad 4 is an iPad-beating tablet in several ways. And the Robot Phone is, well, the Robot Phone. Honor’s products aren’t globally available in the same way as, say, Apple's or Samsung’s, but those who have tried the brand’s phones and tablets will know about their level of hardware quality.
 Phones Innovation of the Year
 Honor Robot Phone 
 Sticking with Honor, it’s hard to see past the Robot Phone as the most exciting Phones Innovation of the Year in 2026. There's been some competition from foldables in this area this year, but Honor deserves credit for bringing something wildly different to the market (in China, at least). Will we ever see the Robot Phone and its fully motorized mechanical gimbal arm in Western markets? I doubt it — but that doesn’t make it any less exciting.
 Read our Honor Robot Phone hands-on 
 Best Value Phone
 Motorola Edge 70 Fusion 
 The Motorola Edge 70 Fusion is in another world for pure value compared to most phones — for example, compared to the iPhone 17e, it costs almost exactly half the price and offers an extra camera, a much larger battery, faster charging, and a higher display refresh rate. The Edge 70 Fusion is not a flashy phone, but it certainly punches above its budget price tag.
 Best Mid-Range Phone
 Apple iPhone 17 
 The Apple iPhone 17 is over 12 months old now (it just slips into this year’s eligibility window), and it wasn’t replaced with a successor in September — but it didn’t need to be. With its 120Hz refresh rate, two great rear cameras, powerful A19 chipset, and still-industry-leading Center Stage selfie camera, the iPhone 17 is still the iPhone we recommend to most people.
 Best Folding Phone
 Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 
 The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the only globally available passport-shaped foldable we’ve tested fully (and that's eligible for this year's awards), and it's earned our pick as the Best Folding Phone of the year. We were skeptical about the practicality of the Z Fold 8’s stumpy form factor, but after living with the phone for a month , we came around to its charming oddness.
 Read our full Samsung Galaxy Z fold 8 review 
 Best Flip Phone
 Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 
 The Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 (or Motorola Razr 70 Ultra, as it’s called in certain regions) is, for us, the best phone you can buy in this category. The Galaxy Z Flip 8 has better software, a newer chipset, and is slightly more affordable — but the latest Razr Ultra has a larger battery, faster charging, and better cameras. It’s a close-run thing, but this is the flip phone we'd choose.
 Best Camera Phone
 Oppo Find X9 Ultra 
 The Oppo Find X9 Ultra is an absolute beast of a camera phone. It boasts a 200MP main lens, a 50MP ultra-wide lens, a 200MP 3x telephoto lens, and a 50MP 10x telephoto (f/3.5) lens, which is a combination that helped it beat the Galaxy S26 Ultra and hold its own against even the Lumix TZ300 and Nikon Z8 in our head-to-head comparisons. It’s heavy, thick, and eye-wateringly expensive, but the Find X9 Ultra is the closest we’ve come to a truly camera-rivaling smartphone.
 Read our full Oppo Find X9 Ultra review 
 Best Gaming Phone
 RedMagic 11 Pro 
 If you’re looking for an unashamedly gamer-y smartphone, it doesn’t get much better than the RedMagic 11 Pro. With its exposed water-cooling system, capacitive shoulder buttons, powerful Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset, and gorgeous 6.85-inch OLED display, it’s more handheld console than phone.
 Read our full RedMagic 11 Pro review 
 Best AI Phone
 Google Pixel 11 Pro 
 Even though Google’s latest Pixel series doesn’t bring much newness to the table, it’s hard to argue against the Pixel 11 Pro’s status as the Best AI Phone money can buy. There’s Camera Coach, Magic Cue, Magic Editor, Magic Capture, Rambler, and, of course, system-wide Gemini integration to take advantage of with Google’s latest flagship. If AI is your jam, the Pixel 11 Pro should be your phone.
 Read our full Google Pixel 11 Pro review 
 Best Phone Accessory
 DJI Osmo Mobile 8P 
 Phone gimbals aren’t the flashiest products around, but the DJI Osmo Mobile 8P deserves credit for being one of the best phone accessories money can buy. As we noted in our review, the 8P adds a remote control and even better tracking capabilities to the already impressive Osmo Mobile 8 formula, and as such, it’s an easy recommendation for content creators.
 Read our full DJI Osmo Mobile 8P review 
 Best Tablet
 Honor MagicPad 4 
 The Android tablet market is a real mix of good, bad, and terrible right now, but the Honor MagicPad 4 surprised us by being a genuinely iPad-rivaling slate in testing this year. For a lower price than the latest iPad Air, the MagicPad 4 offers a thin and lightweight design, a stunning OLED screen, an excellent eight-speaker stereo setup, and near-unbeatable update support. Here’s hoping Honor continues its hot streak into 2027.
 Read our full Honor MagicPad 4 review 
 Best eReader
 Amazon Kindle Scribe (2025) 
 The last 12 months have seen plenty of great ereaders and digital note-takers come to market, but the Amazon Kindle Scribe (2025) has become our go-to recommendation for those after an ereader/notebook hybrid. It's pricey, yes, but the Scribe’s 11-inch E Ink Carta 1300 display is a joy to behold.
 Read our full Amazon Kindle Scribe (2025) review 
 Cameras & drones 
 Camera of the Year
 Sony A7R VI 
 Perfect ratings are rare, but the A7R VI earned five stars with its 66.8MP stacked full-frame sensor, image stabilization, new processor and improved subject-detection autofocus, which combine for class-leading quality and performance. Whether you shoot landscape photography or action, the A7R VI can handle it all, and its excellent handling and new and improved battery was the cherry on the cake. Our verdict? "Sony can stop making cameras now."
 Read our full Sony A7R VI review 
 Brand of the Year
 Sony 
 Following a relatively quiet year, Sony has stood out in 2026 with three top cameras and a raft of new lenses. We gave a perfect five-star rating to the Sony A7R VI, which received high praise from our veteran Cameras Editor who said it had "no weaknesses". The A7 V took top spot in our best mirrorless cameras guide, while the RX10 V revived bridge cameras and extended Sony’s lead at the top in this category. Add Sony’s stellar macro lens to the mix and this award was inevitable.
 Camera Innovation of the Year 
 Antigravity A1 
 The Antigravity A1 was a first-of-its-kind drone, one that can shoot true 360 degree video thanks to its dual camera array. The Insta360-backed company effectively gave us an airborne Insta360 X5, with immersive 8K video recording that sees in every direction. At the launch event, we donned the company’s goggles and followed racing cars around a track, and the whole experience was intuitive — but most of all immersive. You don’t need to worry about framing the shot, because that happens later using Insta360’s clever software, which can frame and compile videos after the fact.
 Read our full Antigravity A1 review 
 Best Beginner Camera
 OM System PEN 
 It was a tight call between the OM System PEN and the Lumix L10, but ultimately we felt that the PEN is the better starting point for beginner photographers, at a much lower price point. Not only is the PEN easy on the eye, but it features image stabilization, a rangefinder-style EVF, a weatherproof body, and a host of clever computational photography modes that smartphone upgrades will feel at home with, and that encourage creativity. A huge choice of lenses and a new weatherproof kit lens complete the package. 
 Read our OM System PEN review 
 Best Mid-range camera
 Sony A7 V 
 The mid-range full-frame category is fiercely contested by Canon, Nikon, Sony and Panasonic, but Sony stole back its crown with the new A7 V, in a year that Canon also released the stellar EOS R6 Mark III. Between those two 5-star cameras, we felt the A7 V had the (slight) edge overall; there's nothing to choose in terms of resolution, but the A7 V has a partially stacked sensor for what should be quicker readout speeds, plus snappier subject detection autofocus, wider dynamic range, versatile flip-and-tilt screen, and class-leading battery life. 
 Read our Sony A7 V review 
 Best Professional Camera
 Sony A7R VI 
 It’s actually been a quiet year in the professional camera category, but that's probably good for the other companies, because the A7R VI would’ve been hard for anyone to compete with. It ups the bar with a class-leading 66.8MP full-frame stacked sensor that's backed up with the power, speed and pro-grade body that make the camera a formidable tool in any pro photography scenario. We shot landscape, portrait and wildlife photography, and the pro camera thrived in all situations.
 Read our full Sony A7R VI review 
 Best Compact and Instant Camera
 Ricoh GR IV 
 Being intimately familiar with the GR III, we were super excited about the GR IV launch and the upgrades it would bring. A new 26MP APS-C sensor with five-axis stabilization and improved battery life topped the improvements, but we’ll have to keep fingers crossed for next time for the improved build quality, a tilt screen and built-in-flash we wished for. Even still, the GR IV can shoot the best quality photos from a truly pocketable camera, with a dedicated Monochrome edition that came alter to boot. The price hike stung, but no other brand is making a compact like Ricoh is. 
 Read our Ricoh GR IV review 
 Best Action and Vlogging Camera
 DJI Osmo Pocket 4P 
 It’s been a busy year in this category, with Insta360 and DJI in particular trading blows. First came DJI's Pocket 4, which was a modest upgrade of the Pocket 3, but DJI had something extra special up its sleeve; a twin-lens gimbal camera Pocket 4P, which would change the game for vlogging. Insta360 then tried to steal DJI’s thunder with its innovative Luna Ultra's twin lenses and removable remote module — but DJI's Pocket 4P feels like the more polished of the two, and the one we have found ourselves turning to more often for shooting stabilized 4K content. 
 Read our DJI Osmo Pocket 4P review 
 Best Camera Lens
 Sigma 135mm f/1.4 DG | Art 
 Lenses is a competitive category year after year, and 2025-2026 was no different, with a top Sony macro optic, Nikon's slimmed down 70-200mm f/2.8 and a number of superb-value Viltrox optics. However, we must recognize innovation and give credit where it's due, which is why Sigma’s first 135mm telephoto lens with a f/1.4 aperture blew us away. Bulky, yes, but we gave it five stars in our review, calling the 135mm F1.4 DG / Art the 'bokeh master' — if you want the dreamiest portraits, look no further.
 Read our Sigma 135mm f/1.4 DG | Art review 
 Best Camera Accessory
 Insta360 Mic Pro 
 DJI and Insta360 have been trading blows all year, but it was Insta360’s Mic Pro that was the final piece of the jigsaw for the 360 camera maker’s ecosystem. Insta360 fans using the likes of the class leading X6 360-degree camera, Ace Pro 2 action cam and Luna Ultra vlogging cameras can enjoy all the benefits of direct compatibility with one of the best wireless mics we’ve ever tested — mixing and matching their camera with a third party mic is no longer necessary. And what a mic it was — the Mic Pro has DJI-beating noise cancellation and an eye-catching, customizable e ink display. 
 Read our Insta360 Mic Pro review 
 Best Drone
 DJI Avata 360 
 First came the Antigravity A1 drone, and then came the DJI Avata 360, which felt like the more polished and versatile 360-degree drone of the two. Where the A1 has two fixed lenses to capture 360-degree footage, the Avata 360’s twin lenses are mounted to a gimbal which can rotate 90 degrees to switch between regular (front-facing) single-lens and top/bottom facing 360-degree use. The product also joins DJI's existing Avata ecosystem, which already includes superb FPV goggles and motion controller accessories. Bottom line — the A1 came first, but the Avata 360 upped the bar, and it costs much less. 
 Read our DJI Avata 360 review 
 Computing 
 Laptop of the Year
 Apple MacBook Neo 
 If there's one laptop that has made the biggest impact in 2026, then it's the MacBook Neo. When Apple announced its brand-new MacBook earlier this year, along with the impressively-affordable starting price of $599 / £599 / AU$1,049, it sent shockwaves through the industry. That might sound like hyperbole, but by releasing a budget laptop that still features a premium-feeling (and looking) design and without too many compromises when it comes to features and performance, the MacBook Neo shook rival PC makers out of their complacency and got them to up their budget laptop game. We had numerous laptop makers freely admit that they were releasing $600 laptops to challenge the MacBook Neo. For the sheer impact alone, the MacBook Neo has to be our pick as laptop of the year.

 The best Fitbits were among the first high-quality fitness trackers, an upgrade to the pedometer, when they first launched almost 20 years ago. Since then, the brand's innovations have meant women can track almost every part of their wellbeing from their wrist.
 Now, with Google’s buyout powering smarter features, deeper health insights, and a brand new app for tracking your data, the Fitbit ecosystem feels more advanced than ever.
 I’ve spent the past five years testing the best fitness trackers and smartwatches. I know what separates a good device from a great one, from comfort and battery life to health metrics and everyday usability. Below, I’ve rounded up the latest Fitbits and ones still worth buying today, plus the information you need to choose one that suits you.
 Recent updates 
 27/10/2026: With the release of the Google Fitbit Edge and Fitbit Air, the new Google Health App, and the Google Pixel Watch 5, I have updated this guide after thorough testing over several weeks with each device.
 The quick list

 The Fitbit Edge finds the perfect middle ground between the Fitbit Air and Google Pixel Watch 5, making it the top pick for affordability and features. There are no compromises, and I'd recommend this watch to anyone, regardless of fitness level or health goal, as the Edge can help you do it all.

It's also only one of two traditional Fitbits with an ECG monitor (the other is the Charge 6), alongside the regular fitness, sleep, and stress insights.

 - Some smart features need a phone connection
 With its oval-shaped, high-resolution screen, comfortably flush design, improved GPS and heart rate tracking, and brilliant smartwatch features, the Fitbit Edge notches out the Fitbit Air to the top spot to round out the year.
 I took this watch for a spin over two weeks, and I was so impressed. While there are few new features for fitness or sleep obsessives, the Edge covers these insights brilliantly with over 100 workout profiles to choose from. You can set these manually, or the watch will automatically record basic sports like walking and running. You'll find a Smart Wake Alarm to gently wake you in your lightest sleep phase, along with deep insights into your rest and activity in the Google Health app.
 While you'll need to keep your phone connected to reap its smart features (including full remote music control, timers, Google Maps connectivity and more), this wasn't a problem for me, and I made full use of them.
 For under £160, this watch is a real steal and the ideal gift for fitness lovers in your life.
 Google released this watch in October 2026, making it the third release of the year after the Pixel 5 and Fitbit Air, which also feature in this guide. It's the perfect middle ground between the affordable, screenless Air and the premium, advanced Pixel 5. That said, it's a brilliant fitness tracker in its own right.

 Reasons to avoid
 - AI suggestions not always accurate
 The Fitbit Air looks a little different from the other best Fitbits. Being screenless, all the data is available to view in the new Google Health app , which you can use for free (but I'd recommend a premium membership to make the most of it). It was refreshing not to have all my data at my fingertips, buzzing at me when I didn't move. Instead, I could let it work in the background and still get all the insights to make lifestyle changes.
 The AI integration with Google's Gemini is the standout feature, however. As someone who has been regularly exercising for years, I like to think I know what I'm doing. The Fitbit Air was a fascinating takedown of that. Using insights from your vitals (e.g. heart rate and breathing rate), exercise history, sleep and stress data, and your goals, the AI delivered a smattering of health insights into my app throughout the day. It also suggested a workout plan and better sleep routines, based on this data.
 However, it also works like a regular Fitbit. The Fitbit Air picks up on your steps, workouts, and sleep, logging everything tidily in the app. It balances advanced technology and insights with easy use in a way that few other fitness trackers, let alone Fitbits, do.
 When it comes to reviewing fitness trackers, my standards are very high. I've tested close to 100 over the last few years, from Garmin watches and Apple Watches to other faceless trackers like the Oura Ring. This is the only one I've ever given five stars to.

 The Fitbit Charge 6 comes in a very close second in my ranking for an original Fitbit. It's a brilliant running watch for beginners, but anyone looking to get fitter will find it ticks all the boxes for logging workouts, recording daily activity, and keeping a close eye on sleep.
 There are 40 workout modes to choose from - from running to paddleboarding - and step count, stress, and sleep tracking, along with Bluetooth connectivity to most machines from major brands like Peloton, NordicTrack, and Concept2. This means I can get a direct-to-wrist feed from the machine during my workout, recording my distance, pace, and more without an issue.
 You won't miss out on the smartwatch features you'd get on the other models either. The Fitbit Charge 6 has almost complete Google connectivity - unlike other Fitbits on the market. I can access Google Maps, Google Wallet, and YouTube Music from the watch face, making my daily walks to buy coffee easier, as well as my longer runs.
 While the small rectangular screen doesn't allow for a huge amount of viewing space, compared to the Fitbit Edge, for example, it's enough to see the essentials.

 While the Google Pixel Watch 5 design remains the same as the Pixel Watch 4 , its great new health and fitness features make it well worth the upgrade for any Fitbit users looking to graduate to a smartwatch.
 It offers all you need to track daily activity and workouts, with deep insights in the new Google Health app. The app's premium subscription can also help improve your exercise routine with AI-created workout suggestions and insights. If it's a cardio workout, you can send the session straight to the device and follow along. I'm expecting the brand to launch the same for strength workouts soon as well.
 The smartwatch features take it a notch above the rest, however. Proactive Suggestions take your location, calendar, and routine into account and bring up useful suggestions (like your work calendar when you arrive at the office or your train ticket when you get to the station), cutting out the need for your phone in my circumstances. The Double Tap feature isn't new to the Watch 5, but it's certainly improved. I've greatly enjoyed tapping my fingers to complete hands-free tasks like starting a workout, answering a text or call, and much more. And of course, the built-in Gemini digital assistant helps all this along.
 The only downside? Battery life only lasts up to 30 hours with typical use, which is dramatically lower compared to the Fitbits on this list, which last over a week.

 If you're looking for a simple watch that covers the basics of fitness tracking, you can't go wrong with the Fitbit Inspire 3. It covers the essentials on a (very) small rectangular watch face, including step count, heart rate, calorie burn, and 20 workout modes with SmartTrack, so you can still record your workout even if you forget to press 'start'. Of these, it's possible to store 6 options on the device, but I found these was more than enough.
 It also has SpO2 (blood oxygen) level sensors and a 'Relax' function that takes you through a short meditation or mindful moment using buzzing to control your breathing. That's as advanced as it gets. Unlike the Fitbit Charge 6, the Inspire 3 doesn't have built-in GPS so you'll need to make sure your phone is connected to your watch when you're on the move.
 This is the most basic Fitbit since the Fitbit Luxe , which I also tested before it sold out everywhere a few years ago. It's not going to support you through more than your daily 10,000 steps and perhaps a 5km run, but at less than £90 at full RRP and often much less on sale, it's hardly one to complain about. After testing it myself for several weeks, it's enough to revamp your fitness routine and inspire a lifestyle change if you're new to exercise.

 6. Fitbit Sense 2

 Reasons to avoid
 - Most expensive Fitbit on the list
 While I would recommend my top pick, the Fitbit Edge, for health tracking overall, the Sense 2 is a good second option. Its main benefit is the larger screen. Along with the Charge 6 and the Edge, it's only one of three Fitbits with the advanced ECG sensor. This looks out for any irregularities in your heart rate and can be used to potentially flag issues that you can discuss with your doctor.
 It's also great for sleep insights. You can scroll across the touchscreen to view your sleep insights on the Sense 2, making it the best Fitbit for those prioritising learning how to sleep better this year. You can see your overall sleep duration and your sleep score for the night, and with the 6 months of free Fitbit Premium that comes with the device, you can view your Sleep Profile on the device too. Provided you wear the Sense 2 for at least 14 days a month, you'll see your main sleep characteristics on your wrist whenever you like.
 Generally, in testing, I found the Sense 2 smartwatch prioritises complete wellbeing over fitness-specific achievements. Along with improved sleep analysis, there are advanced sensors: blood glucose tracking, an EDA scan app for advanced stress management, and Sp02 blood oxygen level tracking. These are useful for overall health monitoring and great for anyone looking to improve their fitness through better recovery rates, on the lookout for irregular heart rhythms, or monitoring their breathing rate. These are not included in many older versions of the Fitbit, but they do feature on the Fitbit Versa 3 and 4, so it's worth comparing the Fitbit Sense 2 vs Versa 4 before making a final decision.
 Along with all these advanced features, it does the basics very well. I found I could start and navigate through any one of the 40+ workout modes with ease and it's still easy to use with a simple navigation system. The addition of a side button was a welcome return, and there is a dedicated page for the element of fitness tracking most important to you, whether that's steps done, calories burned, distance covered, and so on, so you can prioritise what's important to you.
 Read our full review of the Fitbit Sense 2 here. 
 How I tested the best Fitbits 
 After consulting the experts on important factors to consider, I tested each Fitbit over several weeks through various workouts, from strength training to spin classes, hiking, running, and more daily activities, assessing each model on a range of factors that impact day-to-day use.
 Kate Rowe-Ham , a level 3 qualified personal trainer, specialist women's health coach, and founder of Owning Your Menopause , was one of the professionals I spoke to during testing for many of these watches. She is also a fan of the brand. "These devices allow you to track important benchmarks in your fitness, like your daily step count. Once you can see how you're doing in various areas each day, such as your sleep and activity, you have a clear benchmark to improve on moving forward," she says. "As the saying goes, what gets measured gets managed, and over time, you'll be able to spot any trends that may be affecting your wellbeing."
 When testing the best Fitbits, I considered the following: 
 How easy it was to use: A tracker that charges quickly, has a long-lasting battery life, and is easy to navigate during sweaty workouts is key. It's where screen size and responsivity play a huge role, so I tested to see how easy each of the best Fitbits was to use.
 How comfortable it was to wear: I noted how comfortable each of the smartwatches and trackers was to wear - no one wants a wristband that rubs uncomfortably against the skin or catches on clothing after all.
 The features it offers: There are so many Fitbit models out there now - some people will want a Fitbit that offers features such as contactless payment, on-screen text messages, and music streaming. Others might want a Fitbit that tracks daily activity and sleep patterns, so we've tested a range of the best Fitbits with different features.
 Accuracy of heart-rate monitoring: More advanced models will be able to track in more detail, comparing where your current heart rate sits against your usual maximal heart rate (MHR) to assess how hard you’re working at any given point.
 Waterproofing: Most Fitbit models are swimproof and waterproof to 50m but this is important to consider. "If swimming forms a part of your exercise routine, or even if it's just a recreational activity you enjoy," he says.
 Built-in or smartphone GPS: "Some models include GPS built-in, which is more accurate for tracking distance than devices that use an accelerometer, such as many smartphones."
 I also tested... 
 I've tested many other Fitbit devices over the last five years, including the Fitbit Versa 4 . It's a great Fitbit and was on this list until the release of the Fitbit Edge and Pixel Watch 5. These releases meant the Versa's smartwatch features were no longer progressive or original. I also found the fitness, sleep, and health tracking features on more affordable, newer models.
 I also tested the Fitbit Charge 5 , Versa 3 , Fitbit Luxe, Charge 4 , the Inspire 2, and the Google Pixel Watch 3 . However, either these devices are no longer available to buy online, it's been surpassed by other features on newer models, or it's still available but I'd consider it overpriced for the features in 2026.
 Last year, Google announced that it would no longer produce new versions of the Fitbit Versa or the Fitbit Sense, the brand's original smartwatches, choosing instead to focus on the Pixel line-up.
 Over the years, I've tested older Fitbits and reviewed them for this guide, including the Fitbit Versa 3 and Charge 5. 
 (Image credit: Grace Walsh/Future)
 Are Fitbits waterproof? 
 All of the best Fitbits are water-resistant up to 50 meters. "They're designed to be swim-proof and stand up to even the sweatiest of workouts," the brand says, making them perfect for exploring all the benefits of swimming . However, no Fitbit will be suitable for diving or deeper submersion than this, and the brand warns against wearing the device in any warm environment, like a hot tub or sauna.
 Some Fitbits, such as the Versa 3, have a swim lock so you can go swimming or take the device in the shower without an issue. Having the swim lock enabled isn't essential. It will prevent the water from acting on the touchscreen and navigating around the watch accidentally. Most settings and metrics are controlled via the app, like changing the time on a Fitbit , so you don't have to worry about these being impacted by the water.
 Some straps are also not water-resistant but can withstand sweat. These include:
 Woven straps (Sense and Versa 3)
 Hook and Loop bands (Charge 5)
 Knit bands (Sense and Versa 3)
 If you want a completely water-resistant band, opt for the Infinity band that comes included when you buy one of the best Fitbits, or the Sports band, which is more breathable.

 You don’t need to wait until Black Friday to lock in an epic deal on one of the year’s best smartwatches . The Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED is my go-to smartwatch for outdoor adventures, and now it can be yours, too, for $100 off retail.
 That’s right: this rugged, LED flashlight-sporting, battery-life champion is $349 on Amazon , down from $449, a seriously good price, and not far from its lowest-ever sale price of $299.
 That said, if you want the best deal on the Garmin Instinct 3, it may be worth holding out a little longer. Of course, as with everything in life, nothing is guaranteed. But I digress.
 I wear the Garmin Instinct 3 while running, walking , hiking , biking , e-mountain biking , snowboarding , snorkeling, and more. Aside from reliable tracking accuracy and excellent battery life, here are the three biggest reasons it’s one of my all-time favorite wearables.
 Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED: was $449 now $349 at Amazon The Garmin Instinct 3 is a tough-built smartwatch with 100 meters of water resistance, a bright AMOLED screen, crazy-good battery performance, and a handy onboard LED flashlight. Tracking accuracy is rock-solid, and Garmin’s sleep/recovery insights are among the best in the business. 
 View Deal 
 Rugged, waterproof design
 Most smartwatches offer just 50 meters of water resistance, enough protection for hand-washing and surface-level swims, but not high-impact water sports or scuba diving. However, similar to the Apple Watch Ultra 4 , the Garmin Instinct 3 is rated for 100 meters of water resistance, so feel free to splash around.
 The Instinct 3 also has an impact-resistant, metal-reinforced bezel that offers ample protection from bumps and drops. Meanwhile, five well-sized physical buttons make the Garmin a breeze to navigate, even with sweaty hands or gloves on.
 (Image credit: Dan Bracaglia/Tom's Guide) Bright AMOLED screen
 The Instinct 3 comes in several different flavors, including your choice of either a bright and well-saturated AMOLED screen or a duller-looking, monochromatic MIP display with solar charging. The advantage of the latter is better battery performance.
 However, I’m a firm believer that the AMOLED variant is the better option because the screen is far more readable in a wider range of scenarios, including bright sunlight. Then again, when wearing polarized sunglasses, MIP has the advantage over AMOLED. Good thing the Garmin Instinct 3 Solar is also on sale for $50 off via Amazon right now.
 Onboard LED flashlight
 (Image credit: Dan Bracaglia/Tom's Guide) Finally, the Instinct 3 is the first smartwatch I’ve tested with a powerful LED flashlight built into the case, but now I wish every smartwatch had one.
 The LED "torch" is so subtle, it’s easy to miss, that is, until you turn it on. At its top output, this small but mighty flashlight is powerful enough to light your way in utter darkness. It also has a strobe mode as well as a red light mode, useful when stargazing.

Battery life is solid rather than show-stopping, but our reviewer still comfortably got through a full day, even with sleep tracking enabled, and fast charging helps take some of the sting out of daily top-ups.

 How to choose the best smartwatch for iPhone 
 Choosing the best smartwatch for your iPhone requires you to think about compatibility, features, and your priorities. The first thing to consider is compatibility. The Apple Watch is the best smartwatch for most people with an iPhone. It’s designed to work seamlessly with iOS and it offers great integration with Apple’s ecosystem. Features like notifications, messaging, Apple Pay, and health data syncing all work incredibly well. If you want the most out of your smartwatch, for most people an Apple Watch is the top choice.
 Consider the features you need the most. The Apple Watch offers a range of fitness and health tracking, including heart rate monitoring, ECG, sleep tracking, and blood oxygen levels. Newer models now offer even more advanced features, like body temperature tracking. But if health and fitness aren’t your priority, many of the watches in the guide above offer support for notifications, app interactions, and even cellular connectivity for use without your phone.
 The Apple Watch is considered the gold standard for iPhone users, but other options, like Fitbit or Garmin smartwatches, also work very well with iOS. You may find that they don’t offer the same level of integration but do bring you excellent health tracking features and longer battery life. So if you're primarily looking for a fitness tracker with basic notification functionality, these can be great alternatives.
 A downside of the Apple Watch, at least compared to some other brands, is its battery life. It typically lasts a day or two. This means that if you prioritize longer-lasting battery life over advanced features, you may want to consider alternatives from other brands, like Garmin, which can last longer on a single charge, depending on the model.
 Since you’re going to be wearing it most of the time, the design of the smartwatch for iPhone you choose will be a crucial factor. Apple Watches come in a range of sizes and you can customize them with interchangeable bands, which makes it easy to find a style that suits you. Other smartwatch brands also offer nice-looking and comfortable designs, but depending on your preferences, Apple has the edge in terms of aesthetics and comfort.
 For the best overall experience, especially if you have a lot of other Apple products, an Apple Watch is the clear winner. However, if you’re looking for specific features, like extended battery life or more focused fitness tracking, other brands can still offer a solid experience for your iPhone.
 How we test the best smartwatches for iPhone 
 Our smartwatch process typically involves using the device as if it were our own personal wearable. That's the best way for us to fully test it and see how it fares in the real world. We do a comprehensive sweep of its features, functionalities, performance, battery life, and ease of use, doing so over multiple days.
 Of course, since we also want to know how it performs and which features are available when it's paired with an iPhone, we make sure to squeeze that into our testing as well. Once we've collected all the data and information we need, we take all of it and compare it to the smartwatch's price, finding out if it's a great value for our readers before making a recommendation.
 FAQs 
 What's the best smartwatch for iPhone users?
 The best smartwatch for iPhone users is the one that fits your budget and what you expect it to do; at the time of writing, the Apple Watch Series 11 is our best overall pick for its balance of iPhone integration, display, health tools and everyday usefulness. If you want longer battery life and more structured training tools, the Garmin Venu X1 may suit you better, while the Amazfit Active 2 is our budget option.
 We regularly update this guide as we test and review new watches, so the best overall pick can change. If you are not ready to buy yet, bookmark this page and return when you are comparing current models and prices.
 Should I buy an Apple Watch or a Garmin for my iPhone?
 Buy an Apple Watch if you want a watch that feels like an extension of your iPhone. Setup takes minutes, notifications arrive without fuss, and things such as Apple Pay, calls and apps work in the way you’d expect. For everyday convenience – checking a message on the train, paying for coffee or leaving your phone in your pocket – it’s hard to beat.
 Garmin is the better fit if your watch is primarily a training companion and the thought of another nightly charge makes you groan. The Venu X1 works with iPhone, brings maps, Garmin Coach and Training Readiness, and can last up to nine days with its always-on display off. You sacrifice some of Apple’s polish, but gain the sort of endurance and workout depth keen runners and cyclists will appreciate.
 What is the best budget smartwatch for iPhone users?
 The Amazfit Active 2 is our current best budget smartwatch for iPhone users because it packs in far more than its price suggests. It has a bright AMOLED display, a light, classic-looking design, strong GPS and workout tracking, plus an onboard AI assistant – plenty of useful smartwatch basics, without the usual Apple Watch outlay.
 In our testing, it was comfortable to wear and its calorie and workout figures held their own against an Apple Watch Ultra 2. Amazfit says it can manage five days of heavy use, too, which is a welcome break from daily charging. Want the full watchOS experience and closer iPhone integration? Spend more on the Apple Watch SE 3; the Active 2 is for buyers who want plenty of watch for less.
 Do non-Apple smartwatches work with an iPhone?
 Yes – you are not locked into an Apple Watch just because you own an iPhone. Garmin, Amazfit and Huawei watches can pair through their companion apps, delivering notifications, activity tracking and health or workout data. 
 The catch is that the experience is rarely as joined-up. Third-party watches can be great for fitness and endurance, but app interaction, replying to messages, calls, payments and data syncing may be more limited. Check the companion app supports your iPhone and current iOS version, then make sure the features you actually use are on the list before clicking buy.
 Do Apple Watch health features work in every country?
 No. Apple Watch health features are not a one-size-fits-all deal: availability can vary by country, model, software version and local regulations. ECG, blood oxygen and hypertension notifications are among the features that can differ, so a watch bought in one market may not have exactly the same health toolkit in another.
 If a particular health feature is your reason for buying, check Apple’s current watchOS feature-availability page for your country before handing over your money. And while these tools can be useful for spotting trends or prompting a conversation, they are not a substitute for medical advice – speak to a clinician if you receive an alert or have a concern.

 Design : The Series 12 carries forward the Series 11 's sleek design, featuring a bright and colorful 2,000-nit wide-angle OLED display. The aluminum models have a new Ceramic Shield front cover for extra durability, and the Series 12 offers a lot of size, material, and finish options. You can get 42mm or 46mm sizes in aluminum, titanium, or ceramic, each in a range of colors and with different band options to suit your needs.
 Lifestyle features : Siri AI is built into the watch and can answer general knowledge questions and pull from personal context info, like looking up your driver's license number from your email. WatchOS 27 also delivers more workout guidance and perimenopause and menopause tracking.
 Battery life : The S11 chip and the redesigned health-sensing system work efficiently, giving the Series 12 a real-world battery boost compared with the Series 11. In testing, it lasted for 54.5 hours with the always-on display enabled and with one tracked exercise with GPS each day.
 Who It's For
 Apple fans : The Series 12 combines all of Apple's best wearable features into an attractive package that helps you stay connected, monitor your health, and track your fitness.  Health obsessives : The new health-sensing system keeps tabs on your heart rate constantly, whether you're working out or not.  Pick a Watch That Works With Your Phone
 Naturally, the first thing to consider before purchasing a smartwatch is its compatibility. We include these details in our reviews of each product.
 All Apple Watch models run watchOS , Apple's smartwatch operating system, and work only with iOS devices. Apple's latest wearables—the Series 12, Ultra 4, and Watch SE 3—require an iPhone 11 or later with iOS 27 or later and do not work with Android handsets.
 Samsung's latest smartwatches, the Galaxy Watch 9 and the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, run Wear OS 7 with Samsung's One UI 9 interface. They require a smartphone running Android 13.0 or later. Although you can pair the Galaxy Watch with non-Samsung Android phones, some features are only compatible with Samsung handsets, including AI coaching, irregular heart rhythm notifications, phone separation alerts, gesture controls, and the Camera Controller app.
 Google's Pixel Watch 5 runs Wear OS 7 and is compatible with most phones running Android 12 or later via the Google Pixel Watch app, which requires a Google Account to login in. It's not exclusive to Pixel phones and should pair just fine with devices from any other Android phone maker, including Samsung. That said, some Pixel Watch features are only available when paired with a Pixel phone, including proactive suggestions from Gemini, Ask to Hold for calls, automatic call screening, and the camera controller.
 Most of the other smartwatches on this list are compatible with both Android and iOS smartphones.
 Which Platform Offers the Best Smartwatch Apps?
 What separates a smartwatch from a dumb watch? Many things, but as  smartphones  have taught us, apps may be the most important.
 Most of the watches we like feature full-fledged app stores that bring everything from Spotify, Yelp, and Strava to your wrist. As with smartphones, app availability is a good indicator of which product to choose, so be sure to check each watch's app selection before making a final decision.
 If you're looking for apps, Apple is your best bet. The App Store allows you to browse and download third-party watchOS apps directly on your watch, including popular favorites such as AllTrails, Calm, Pandora, Peloton, Shazam, Spotify, Starbucks, and Strava.
 The Apple Watch still has the largest number of high-quality apps and big-name developers, but Google's Wear OS platform is catching up.
 Samsung's latest smartwatches feature popular Google apps, such as Maps and the Play Store, as well as Samsung's Buds Controller, Pay, and more. The Pixel Watch features all the Google standbys, including Assistant, Gmail, Home, Maps, the Play Store, and Wallet.
 Other popular apps available for download via the Google Play Store on Wear OS smartwatches include Amazon Music, Calm, Deezer, Easy Voice Recorder, KakaoTalk, Samsung Internet Browser, SmartThings, Spotify, Stocard, Todoist, and WhatsApp. 
 How Are Smartwatches Different Than Fitness Trackers?
 Unless you want a gadget on both wrists (not the best look), you should choose a smartwatch that also functions as a fitness tracker . Most smartwatches can track basic activity, such as steps, but you need to pay close attention to their additional features.
 Most of the smartwatches on our list feature GPS connectivity, allowing them to record your runs without a companion device. Most modern smartwatches also have an optical heart rate sensor that can take continuous and on-demand heart rate measurements.
 Fitbit Versa devices are reasonably affordable and track a wide range of fitness and sleep metrics. However, they have fewer third-party apps, so there are some trade-offs. Look closely and choose a watch that tracks the activities and health metrics you want to monitor. Some smartwatches offer advanced health-tracking features, including the ability to take an ECG and measure your SpO2 level.
 Which Smartwatches Have Cellular and Are They Worth the Money?
 A cellular connection allows you to make calls, send texts, stream music, download apps, and do anything else that requires an internet connection—all without your phone. The cellular Apple Watch Series 12 carries a $100 premium over the base model (Bluetooth and Wi-Fi only) and supports 5G for faster downloads. Still, you have to pay for a separate data plan—most carriers charge an additional $10 per smartwatch per month. The Google Pixel Watch 5 and the Galaxy models on this list are also available with cellular connectivity.
 Whether this convenience is worth it for you depends on how you plan to use your watch. If you want to stream music while you exercise and leave your phone at home or in the locker room, a cellular connection can certainly come in handy. If you always have your phone on you, however, you can probably save money and skip it.
 How Long Do Smartwatches Last?
 You don't want a smartwatch with good battery life, right? Good, because you're not going to get it. Features like an always-on display and GPS tracking are nice, but they drain battery life quickly. Watches with full-color, smartphone-like displays, such as the Apple Watch and Wear OS watches, typically last only about a day or two on a charge.
 There are a few exceptions, including the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 and the Apple Watch Ultra 4, which offer three-day battery life. In general, you get much better battery life with a sport-focused Fitbit or Garmin watch. They typically last around six days on a single charge.
 How Much Should You Spend on a Smartwatch?
 Smartwatches can be very expensive, but that doesn't mean you need to spend a lot of money to get a good one. Yes, the $1,000+ Apple Watch Hermès is sure to draw a lot of attention, but for that price, you could buy five Fitbits. If you're a first-time smartwatch buyer, consider the less expensive route first, in case you wind up not wearing it all that much.
 What's the Best Android Watch?
 All the models on this list are compatible with  Android phones, except for the Apple Watch. The Google Pixel Watch 5 is our current favorite thanks to its multi-day battery life, stylish design, and well-implemented AI-based smarts. The Samsung Galaxy Watch series offers a range of options, each packed with wellness features. The Galaxy Watch 9 delivers all of Samsung's latest and greatest health insights, along with a speedy new chip, but its predecessor offers a nearly identical experience for less money. For an even more affordable option, the Samsung Galaxy Watch FE offers a streamlined design, excellent health and safety features, useful calling and texting capabilities, and plenty of value for the money.
 What's the Best-Looking Smartwatch?
 Let's not forget: You'll also be wearing this thing. And unlike your Timex, it's unlikely to remain in style for years. Smartwatch design is rapidly changing, so hold out until you find something you actually want to wear. And keep in mind that smartwatches are still gadgets. The coming year is sure to bring new iterations of pretty much every watch on this list, not to mention completely new ones.
 The battle for wrist real estate is heating up quickly. That's good news for consumers, as this pace of innovation is likely to result in more capable—and stylish—devices. I wouldn't be surprised if this list reads completely differently the next time you see it. But if you're looking for the best smartwatch available today, the options here are the finest we've tested.
 For more, check out our roundups of the best Android watches and the best Samsung watches .

The premium device delivers reliable GPS tracking, advanced health and fitness tools, and improved battery life compared to Samsung’s standard models, all in a durable case meant to handle tough conditions.
 What to look for in a good smartwatch
 Kaitlyn Cimino / Android Authority
 Knowing where to start is not easy if you’re shopping for your first smartwatch. Software experience and compatibility are crucial, but don’t always narrow the field enough. You’ll also want to determine what your priorities are in terms of features and specs.
 The key to finding the right smartwatch is determing your priorities. 
 Do you want an extension of your phone, or are you interested in tracking intense workouts or advanced health stats? Does daily charging sound cumbersome? The topics below are all points I think are worth considering before you commit to any of the smartwatches I’ve recommended in this guide, or generally on the wider market.
 Is it compatible with your phone (Android or iOS)?
 Does it run the latest software version?
 Is the brand renowned for good update consistency?
 What is your budget?
 Does the smartwatch have first- and third-party app support?
 How good is the battery life?
 Does it cater to your fitness tracking needs?
 Does it have onboard or connected GPS (preferably the former)?
 How accurate is the heart rate tracking?
 Does it have SpO2 monitoring?
 Does it have accurate sleep tracking?
 Can it take on-wrist phone calls?
 Is there a voice assistant for hands-free use?
 How does it handle notifications?
 Does it have digital payment support?
 How useful is the companion app (and does it have one at all)?
 Is the fit comfortable?
 Does the look match your aesthetic?
 Why you should trust me
 Kaitlyn Cimino / Android Authority
 I’ve been professionally testing and reviewing wearables for years, dating back to before Samsung teamed up with Google for the Wear OS we now know and love, and long before Apple launched its first-generation, massive Ultra. I’ve reviewed dozens of smartwatches, fitness trackers, dedicated heart rate monitors, smart rings, sleep trackers, exercise equipment, and health and fitness apps and platforms. In other words, I’ve sweated my way through a ton of products to learn what makes them valuable and what features matter most.
 I've been professionally testing and reviewing wearables for more than five years. 
 At the start of every review, my focus is twofold: user experience and value. First, I approach each product as a typical user, noting everything from comfort and design to performance and features. I fire off texts, download apps, and tap into everything from timers to gesture controls. To dig even deeper, I bring expertise and comparable metrics to the conversation, using tools like heart rate monitors, pedometers, pulse oximeters, and trusted sleep trackers and GPS devices. I create varied workout plans to test fitness tracking accuracy and closely monitor my stress and sleep to review recovery metrics.
 Above all, I wear the device consistently to garner a thorough understanding of what it offers and what it’s like to own. I also simultaneously use competitors’ products to compare differences and collect comparative data.

This means establishing its place in the larger market and determining whether its price is fair for what it offers. If a product boasts a large feature set but doesn’t deliver accuracy, it may not be worth its price.  Frequently Asked Questions 
 What's the best smartwatch for women?
 We've got a more detailed entry on this topic below , but in short, for the most part there are no major differences between smartwatches for women and men.
 That said, size may be a favor here, so you may prefer to look for a model that's designed for smaller wrists, such as Garmin's Lily range. 
 Some smartwatches also provide features specific to women's health, although in other cases these are options available within the platform you're using and are not restricted to particular models; Apple Watch Series 8 or later, including the Series 11 and Apple Watch Ultra models...
 How do you charge a smartwatch?
 Unlike smartphones, most smartwatches tend to use a proprietary charger, often a magnetic one. Though they are always included with the watch, this can be frustrating if you lose yours or it breaks. 
 Some chargers will work for multiple models – for instance many Garmins and most Apple Watches are capable of using the same charger, although some older chargers may not be as fast as newer ones. Some can also be charged wirelessly either using Wireless PowerShare from a phone or the Qi standard; check your specific model for details. 
 Which model you use, you should generally remove it from the charger once it’s full; though most devices will have built-in safety features to prevent overcharging, leaving your watch on charge for too long could still degrade the device's lithium-ion battery over time.
 How to set the time on a smartwatch
 Unlike with a non-smart watch, setting the time on a smartwatch is simply a matter of syncing the device to your phone via Bluetooth, using the relevant app. The smartwatch will then take the time from the phone.
 What's the best military smartwatch?
 Several of the best rugged smartwatches are also good choices for military use, and you can also buy plenty of non-smart watches from the likes of Casio that have many useful features for the military including top-notch weatherproofing, long battery life, night-vision backlighting and more. 
 Focusing solely on smart models, Garmin offers a range of ‘Tactical Edition’ watches with ‘stealth’ mode, ballistics information (like a compass/golf watch, that takes wind and weapon range into account) and a quick-wipe ‘kill switch’.
 How does a smartwatch measure sleep?
 Smartwatches are a great way to track the duration and quality of your sleep. Whatever the model, a smartwatch will use heart-rate variability information and motion detection to estimate sleep stages and quality – with varying degrees of accuracy.
 Some smartwatches, such as the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 and the latest Apple Watch models, including the Series 11 and Ultra 3, even have advanced features such as sleep apnea detection.
 How do you set up a smartwatch?
 How you set up your smartwatch will depend on which model you have, but all will follow a roughly similar process.
 In almost all cases you'll follow instructions to sync the smartwatch to your phone – either by scanning the watch with your phone’s camera if using an Apple Watch, or by downloading an app – and will then follow instructions from there.
 Every smartwatch will have its own app, whether Garmin, Pixel, Apple, Polar, Amazfit or any others.
 How to choose the best smartwatch for you 
 Unfortunately, your choice of smartwatch often depends on your choice of phone, as not all wearables are compatible with competitor devices. Apple Watch only works with Apple iPhones. Samsung and Google watches, and other Wear OS devices, only work with Android devices, but you can use a Samsung watch with a Google phone and vice versa.
 Dedicated fitness watches from Garmin, Coros and Polar generally offer much longer battery life than Wear OS or Apple watches, often lasting a week or more between charges. If training is your priority, they're worth considering even if they don't offer the same app ecosystem.
 Most wearables will get about a day of battery life, which will be disappointing if you're converting from a Garmin watch that lasts weeks. You can find a few watches that last longer on this list.
 Finally, smartwatches can be expensive, and frankly, they don't offer much value for what you pay. Before you spring for an Apple Watch Ultra, you might ask if you are really going Scuba diving this year, or if you're just going to check your text messages without disturbing your dinner mates.
 The best smartwatch for women vs men: Is there a difference?
 There are no specific differences when it comes to smartwatches for women or men, and choosing the right one usually comes down to personal preference. 
 One of the main considerations is making sure the watch size fits your wrist. Many smartwatches are quite large, which can feel bulky on slimmer wrists, so it’s worth checking the case size before buying. Many models come in multiple sizes, and when that’s the case, we list the options in our full reviews to help you choose the best fit.
 Some smartwatches also include features focused on women's health. These can include menstrual cycle tracking, ovulation predictions, and symptom logging, often powered by data such as heart rate trends, sleep patterns, and skin temperature. These tools can help provide a broader picture of hormonal cycles and overall well-being.
 This doesn't mean those watches are only designed for women, nor that these features must be used. Most are optional and can be enabled or ignored depending on your preferences.
 If you do plan to use them, it's worth checking the privacy policy of the watch you've bought so you understand where your health data is stored and who can access it.
 Can you use Apple Watch with an Android phone?
 The first thing to check is whether your phone is compatible with the smartwatch you want. You can't use an Apple Watch with an Android phone, as all the functions of watchOS require iOS to interface with. 
 You can't use an Apple Watch with an Android phone, as Apple Watch requires an iPhone for setup and everyday use.
 Likewise, Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch models are designed for Android phones and don't support iPhone. If you regularly switch between Android and iOS, a Garmin, Amazfit or CMF smartwatch is usually a better choice because these work with both platforms.
 How we test smartwatches 
 Every smartwatch on this list has been fully and extensively reviewed by the expert team at TechRadar, so we know exactly what makes them tick.
 Our review process involves using the devices as if they were our own personal wearables, ensuring every smartwatch gets fully tested in the real world. A comprehensive sweep of features takes place, and usage is varied over a week to give us a clear idea of how battery life performs.
 When testing in-house, we generally look at how accurate the GPS is on each smartwatch by testing it against an industry leader such as the Garmin Epix Pro . Likewise for workout metrics. We also rank how usable the watch's operating system is, whether it supports third-party apps, and where it sits in the market. For example, a cheap watch with fewer features is more likely to get four stars than a feature-stuffed premium watch that isn't worth the expensive price.
 Using that knowledge we've then ranked them, factoring in their value, design, features, and performance to get an overall star verdict.

 Not every smartwatch works well with iPhone. Android-first watches often strip out features when paired with iOS, and even some Garmin models lose smart notification support. If you use an iPhone, your options narrow quickly to a shortlist of watches that actually deliver the full feature set.
 We tested five of the best smartwatches for iPhone in 2026, covering everything from the obvious choice (Apple Watch Series 12) to cross-platform picks for runners and health-focused users. Here is where each one lands.
 Before diving in, a note: if you track smart watch apps alongside your device, most of these watches pair well with third-party tools, and we cover the best productivity pairing at the bottom of this guide.

 1. Apple Watch Series 12: Best Overall
 The most capable smartwatch for iPhone, with the deepest iOS integration available. 
 Apple Watch Series 12 launched in September 2026 alongside the iPhone 18 lineup. It runs the new S11 chip and features a redesigned Health Sensing System that reads heart rate every five seconds, a significant upgrade over the 30-second intervals on previous models.
 Blood oxygen monitoring returns globally on Series 12 after being disabled on US models during a patent dispute. The 42mm case starts at $399, with 46mm at $449. Both support 5G cellular on the $100 upgrade tier. Battery life is 18 hours standard, with a 36-hour low-power mode if you need to push through a long day.

A new Max Extended Workout mode runs GPS tracking for up to 45 hours continuously, designed for ultra-endurance events.

 FAQ
 What is the best smartwatch for iPhone in 2026?
 The Apple Watch Series 12 is the best smartwatch for iPhone in 2026. It offers the deepest iOS integration, the most complete health sensor suite, and runs Apple Intelligence features directly on your wrist. Starting at $399, it is the clearest choice for most iPhone users.
 Do Garmin watches work with iPhone?
 Yes, Garmin watches pair with iPhone and provide workout tracking, notifications, and Garmin Connect app features. However, some features are reduced compared to Android: Apple Pay is unavailable, Siri does not work, and smart notification support is limited.  Does Fitbit work with iPhone?
 Yes, Fitbit works with iPhone. You need the Google Health app (formerly Fitbit app) from the App Store. Heart rate, sleep, activity, and workout tracking all sync correctly. Google Wallet and some Google-specific features are Android-only, but the core health tracking works on iOS. More details in our Fitbit and iPhone guide .
 Is Apple Watch Ultra 4 worth it for everyday use?
 For everyday use, the Apple Watch Series 12 or SE 3 will serve you better at a lower price. The Ultra 4's advantages are multi-day GPS tracking, rugged titanium construction, and 50-hour battery life. These benefits are most valuable for endurance athletes and frequent outdoor travelers. For the average iPhone user, $799 is difficult to justify over $399.
 Which Apple Watch should I buy in 2026?
 Buy the Series 12 if you want the best overall experience. Buy the SE 3 if the $399 price point is outside your budget but you still want Apple Watch features.
